mcqs.question: A team wants to reduce their warehouse bill but doesn't know if bytes scanned, compute time, or storage dominates it. Why does this matter before optimizing?
options: It doesn't matter, since all three cost the same amount per unit
Different platforms and pricing models weight the three differently, so optimizing the wrong one (e.g. tuning cluster size when bytes scanned actually dominates) wastes effort
Only storage cost can ever be reduced through optimization
Bytes scanned, compute time, and storage are actually the same underlying metric
mcqs.explanation: Since pricing models weight these three differently, identifying which one actually dominates the bill determines which lever is worth pulling — optimizing compute time when bytes scanned is the real driver wastes effort on the wrong problem. They aren't priced identically, all three are independently optimizable, and they're distinct metrics, not the same thing.

mcqs.question: A materialized view is refreshed every 5 minutes but the underlying dashboard is only viewed twice a day. What's the likely cost issue?
options: No issue — materialized views are always cheaper than running the raw query
Materialized views cannot be refreshed more often than they're queried
This setup guarantees the dashboard will always show stale data
The refresh frequency, which itself consumes compute, may cost more than simply running the raw query on demand for those two daily views
mcqs.explanation: Refreshing a materialized view consumes compute regardless of how often it's actually queried, so refreshing far more frequently than the view is used can cost more than just computing the raw query on demand for those rare views. Materialized views aren't universally cheaper, refresh frequency isn't capped by query frequency, and this setup would actually show fresher (not staler) data than needed.

mcqs.question: Fifty users run the exact same dashboard query against unchanged underlying tables. Which caching layer gives the biggest cost win here, and why?
options: Result cache, since it stores the query's final output and returns it instantly with zero bytes scanned for identical repeat queries against unchanged data
Data cache, since it stores raw data blocks that any query can reuse
Neither cache applies to repeated identical queries
Materialized views, since they are a form of caching
mcqs.explanation: Result cache is keyed on the exact query and underlying table state, so an identical repeated query against unchanged data returns from cache with no re-execution at all — the biggest possible win for this exact scenario. Data cache still requires re-executing query logic, both caches apply here, and materialized views are a distinct mechanism from either caching layer.

mcqs.question: A dashboard query uses SELECT * against a 200-column table but only renders 3 columns, refreshing automatically every few minutes for many viewers. What's the most direct fix?
options: Add more compute nodes to the warehouse cluster
Replace SELECT * with the specific columns actually rendered, directly cutting bytes scanned by roughly the ratio of unused to used columns
Switch the underlying table to row-oriented storage
Increase the materialized view refresh interval
mcqs.explanation: Selecting only the columns actually needed directly and mechanically reduces bytes scanned by close to the ratio of unused to used columns — the cheapest, most direct fix for this exact pattern. Adding compute nodes doesn't address the root cause, switching to row storage would make column-selective reads worse, and this scenario doesn't involve a materialized view.

mcqs.question: According to the comparison of cost levers, why does fixing an unpruned scan pattern typically outperform caching or materialized views for cost reduction?
options: Caching and materialized views are deprecated techniques no longer used
Scan pattern fixes only work on serverless platforms

Fixing scan patterns can yield order-of-magnitude (e.g. 100x) reductions that apply to every execution, while caching only helps repeated/similar queries and materialized views add their own maintenance cost
Caching and materialized views actually increase cost in all cases
mcqs.explanation: Reducing bytes scanned compounds across every execution of a query, often by an order of magnitude, while caching only helps specific repeated patterns and materialized views carry their own refresh cost — making scan-pattern fixes the higher-leverage lever generally. Neither caching nor materialized views are deprecated, scan fixes aren't platform-restricted, and caching/materialized views don't universally increase cost.

mcqs.question: A BI cluster is unused every night but is kept always-on 'to be safe.' What's the direct cost consequence, and what's the fix?
options: No consequence, since always-on clusters cost the same as auto-suspending ones
Always-on clusters cannot be resized once provisioned
The cluster pays for compute during idle overnight hours with no queries running; enabling auto-suspend eliminates that cost with typically only seconds of resume latency
This can only be fixed by migrating to a different platform entirely
mcqs.explanation: An always-on cluster bills for compute time regardless of whether queries are running, so genuine overnight idle time is pure waste that auto-suspend eliminates almost for free, given typically fast resume times. Always-on and auto-suspend clusters do not cost the same, resizing is generally possible on most platforms, and this is a configuration fix, not a platform migration.
